newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe vows to uphold law in Corsica.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe vows to uphold law in Corsica.

text.p: Defying a threat from Corsican separatists, Prime Minister Alain Juippe vowed anew on Friday to firmly apply the law on the Mediterranean island racked by nationalist violence.
"We apply the law. I have nothing else to say, the law will be applied," Juppe told reporters as he left city hall in Bordeaux, southwestern France, where he serves as mayor.
The city hall was hit by a bomb earlier this month in an attack claimed by the "Historic Wing" of the Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC).

In a statement sent to state-owned regional television channel France-3 Corse on Thursday evening, the hardline FLNC had warned Juppe against any attempt to "physically eliminate" its members, saying its response would be extremely violent.
The group said it was referring to investigations launched into a clandestine news conference held by nationalists in the Corsican hills on January 11.

Paris anti-terrorism magistrates had earlier on Thursday opened a probe into the news conference, at which FLNC leaders, surrounded by some 600 hooded and heavily armed men, announced a three-month truce after a wave of bombings.
Some police officers had been nearby, looking on and jotting down license numbers but taking no action.

"Following the threats of arrests concerning the press conference, we declare to the envoy of the Elysee (presidential palace) and the prime minister that our organisation is ready to... explain the conditions under which this conference took place and the response that followed it," the statement said.
The government was reported to have used envoys to conduct secret talks with separatists which failed to resolve their demands for greater autonomy from mainland France.
The statement also cautioned that if the government tried to "physically eliminate" nationalists, then the FLNC would give a response of "incalculable violence".
Juppe has previously decreed a crackdown on violence on the island but there have been few arrests so far.

Frustrated by the failure of the secret negotiations, separatists have taken their battle for autonomy to the mainland in recent weeks, bombing the law courts in Aix-en-Provence and Juppe's mayoral offices in Bordeaux among other targets.

The government has insisted it was on the trail of those responsible for the bombings and would bring them to justice, but island judgges have repeatedly complained that the justice system appeared afraid to take on the Corsican nationalists, known for their determination.

At a French senate colloquium on the situation in Corsica, however, anti-terrorist magistrate Jean-Louis Bruguiere flatly denied that justice was administered differently on the island from elsewhere in France.

"Contrary to what one might think, there is no special treatment for Corsica," said Bruguiere, who is himself handling several investigations involving separatist bombings, including the attack on Juppe's mayoral offices.
"We handle Corsican cases in the same fashion as any other. We must have proof, charges, and so forth -- we must meet our legal obligations," he said.
